case_name: CASE OF ARVANITIS AND PHILELEFTHEROS PUBLIC COMPANY LIMITED v. CYPRUS

assessment.1. Interference with freedom of expressi: There was a clear interference with the applicants’ Article 10 rights. The first applicant, a newspaper columnist, and the second applicant, the publisher, were found liable in civil defamation proceedings and ordered to pay EUR 12,000 plus interest after publication of a political commentary piece in a daily newspaper (see paragraphs 6, 11 and 16). A judicial finding of defamation and an award of damages are classic interferences capable of producing a chilling effect on the press.

assessment.2. Lawfulness and legitimate aim: The interference appears to have been prescribed by law, namely the Cypriot law of defamation and its statutory defences of truth and fair comment (see paragraphs 17-18). It also pursued a legitimate aim, namely the protection of the reputation or rights of others, here C.K.’s personal and professional reputation (see paragraph 9). The decisive issue is therefore whether the interference was necessary in a democratic society.

assessment.3. Context of the speech and margin of a: The impugned article concerned the recovery of Greek-Cypriot property in the occupied areas and the broader Cyprus problem, which the domestic courts themselves accepted was a matter of public interest (see paragraphs 10 and 13). The speech was published in a newspaper opinion column and was intended as commentary on an article already placed in the public domain by C.K. himself in a well-known Greek newspaper (see paragraphs 5-6 and 10). In matters of political or public-interest debate, especially where the press acts as a watchdog, the margin of appreciation is narrow and strong protection is required (see nos. 23556/94, 29369/10, 39954/08, 40660/08 and 60641/08).

assessment.4. Status of the person criticised: Although the domestic courts treated C.K. as a private person (see paragraphs 14 and 16), that assessment seems too restrictive for Article 10 purposes. C.K. was a lawyer active in highly sensitive property litigation connected with the occupation, and at the relevant time he was representing clients in important proceedings abroad (see paragraphs 9 and 12). More importantly, he had voluntarily entered the public arena by publishing his own account of recovering the paintings and by addressing anticipated public criticism in advance (see paragraph 5). Even if he was not a politician, he was not an ordinary private individual wholly outside public debate. Accordingly, he had to display a higher degree of tolerance toward critical press comment than a purely private person would (see nos. 29369/10 and 39954/08).

assessment.5. Facts, value judgments and factual ba: The domestic courts placed decisive weight on the view that C.K. had not literally said that he had bought the paintings or bargained with thieves, and therefore concluded that the article lacked a basis in truth (see paragraphs 12-13 and 16). That approach appears overly formalistic. The core underlying facts were undisputed: C.K. publicly stated that he had recovered one painting by paying money and another through substitution with a forgery, and that he had first tried to recover the second in exchange for money (see paragraph 5). On that basis, the first applicant’s description of the episode as paying a ransom, repurchasing belongings, or negotiating with thieves was a critical interpretation and value judgment, expressed in polemical terms, rather than a precise factual allegation requiring strict proof. Under the Court’s case-law, value judgments do not lend themselves to proof, provided they have a sufficient factual basis, and journalists may use a degree of exaggeration or provocation (see no. 23556/94). Here, the article had such a basis in C.K.’s own published narrative and in the wider public debate described by the applicants (see paragraph 10).

assessment.6. Good faith and responsible journalism: The domestic courts also inferred bad faith from the fact that the first applicant had not contacted C.K. before publication (see paragraphs 12-13). That reason is not fully convincing in the present context. The article was commentary on material already published by C.K. himself; the first applicant relied on C.K.’s own account and sought to express a critical opinion on its implications for a matter of public concern (see paragraphs 5, 6 and 10). While verification duties remain important, Article 10 does not normally require a journalist to seek prior comment from the author of an already public text before publishing a value-laden reaction piece. The domestic courts’ insistence on further enquiries into the exact amount paid and the value of the painting (see paragraph 12) again suggests that they treated rhetorical criticism as if it were a narrowly factual report.

assessment.7. Balancing and proportionality: The national courts acknowledged the public-interest dimension but nevertheless focused mainly on the injury to C.K.’s dignity and professional reputation, the harshness of the language used, and the absence of literal truth in some formulations (see paragraphs 12-16). They did not adequately weigh several factors central to the Strasbourg balance: that the impugned speech contributed to an ongoing public debate; that C.K. had himself stepped into that debate; that the article was recognisably an opinion column; and that the impugned expressions, though caustic and offensive, were closely connected to the subject matter being debated. The sanction was civil rather than criminal, but EUR 12,000 plus interest, imposed jointly and severally on a journalist and newspaper after lengthy proceedings, was still capable of chilling press discussion on a highly sensitive public issue (see paragraphs 11, 15 and 16). In these circumstances, the reasons given by the domestic courts do not appear sufficiently relevant and sufficient to justify the interference under Article 10 (see nos. 39954/08, 40660/08, 60641/08 and 29369/10).

assessment.8. Overall prediction: Taking the case as a whole, the interference was lawful and pursued a legitimate aim, but it was not proportionate to that aim. The domestic courts gave inadequate weight to the press’s role in public-interest debate, treated value judgments too rigidly as facts, and failed to recognise that C.K. had voluntarily exposed his conduct to public scrutiny. The Court would therefore be likely to find a violation of Article 10.
